title: Health misinformation creates an unequal practical-judgment gap between information exposure, confidence, and safe care decisions
source_unit: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, Health Misinformation: Public Perceptions of Threat to the UK, based on Survation survey
geography: United Kingdom adults aged 18+; national online-panel survey conducted 9–10 September 2026

observations.period: September 2026; confidence in evaluating health claims

denominator.unit: UK adults surveyed by Survation through an online panel

low_confidence_accuracy.unit: percent not very or not at all confident judging whether a health claim is accurate

high_confidence_accuracy.unit: percent very or somewhat confident judging whether a health claim is accurate

income_gap.value: 56% of people earning over £40,000 were very or somewhat confident versus 34% earning under £20,000

education_gap.value: 55% with level 4 or higher qualifications were confident versus 34% lacking level 1 qualifications

observations.method: Cross-sectional online-panel survey commissioned and funded by LSHTM and conducted by Survation on 9–10 September 2026.
observations.uncertainty: Confidence is self-reported and is not a test of misinformation detection accuracy; the online-panel design and regional sample-size limits constrain representativeness and causal inference.
observations.subgroup: UK adults by income, educational attainment, age, region, and reported access to health-information resources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower confidence may reflect appropriate caution rather than lower capability, while high confidence does not establish accurate judgment.

observations.period: September 2026; exposure routes and health topics

denominator.unit: UK adults surveyed; exposure responses allowed multiple sources or topics

social_media_exposure.unit: percent who had encountered health information they believed false or misleading on social media

website_blog_exposure.unit: percent reporting websites or blogs as an exposure route

ai_chatbot_exposure.unit: percent reporting AI chatbots as an exposure route

topic_exposure.value: 24% vaccines; 21% dietary supplements or weight-loss injections; 18% climate change; 16% mental health

reproductive_health_young_adults.unit: percent of 18–24 year-olds reporting exposure to misinformation about women's reproductive health

observations.method: Survey questions on prior exposure routes and six-month exposure to specified health misinformation topics; multiple responses permitted.
observations.uncertainty: Exposure is based on respondents' classification of claims as false or misleading; it does not verify claim falsity, exposure frequency, algorithmic causation, or subsequent behavior.
observations.subgroup: UK adults, with age, gender, and regional differences in reported exposure across topics and channels.
observations.counterinterpretation: High social-media exposure may partly reflect greater use and recall, while low reported exposure may reflect recognition gaps rather than safer information environments.

observations.period: September 2026; regretted decisions and known harm

denominator.unit: UK adults surveyed, with age-specific subgroup comparisons

regretted_health_decision.unit: percent reporting a health decision based on false or misleading information later regretted

regretted_18_24.unit: percent of 18–24 year-olds reporting a regretted health decision

known_serious_harm.unit: percent saying someone they knew had come to serious harm after such a decision

known_serious_harm_18_24.unit: percent of 18–24 year-olds reporting someone known had suffered serious harm

family_worry.unit: percent worried family members could be harmed by health decisions based on misinformation

observations.method: Self-reported survey questions about personal regret, known serious harm, and family concerns; examples included preventable disease, delayed treatment, or prolonged symptoms.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not clinically verify harms, identify specific claims, establish timing or causality, or distinguish misinformation from other reasons for a health decision.
observations.subgroup: Young adults, older adults, families, and respondents with different exposure and information-checking practices.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported regret and known harm may increase awareness of misinformation and motivate later checking or demand for trusted information rather than only indicating vulnerability.

observations.period: September 2026; checking behavior and policy legitimacy

denominator.unit: UK adults surveyed; action-priority responses ranked top three of six options

nhs_or_government_check.unit: percent who would check an NHS or government website

gp_or_pharmacist_check.unit: percent who would ask a GP or local community pharmacist

ai_chatbot_check.unit: percent who would ask an AI chatbot

government_more_action.unit: percent saying the UK Government should do more

policy_priorities.value: 57% ranked penalties for those profiting from misinformation, 54% public education, and 46% platform warning labels among their top three priorities

observations.method: Survey of preferred checking routes, perceived effects, government responsibility, and ranked policy priorities.
observations.uncertainty: Preferred actions are legitimacy and attitude measures, not evidence that legislation, education, labeling, or support would reduce misinformation or improve care outcomes.
observations.subgroup: UK adults, public-health institutions, clinicians, platforms, government, families, and people using AI or social media for health information.
observations.counterinterpretation: A mixed response—trusted public sources, clinicians, family, AI, and social media—suggests that information ecosystems require accessible human and institutional handoffs rather than a single corrective channel.

related_sources.claim: LSHTM release summarizing the survey and report launch.
Full LSHTM report with methods, findings, questions, and limitations.

boundary: This record adds a health-information, practical-judgment, and institutional-trust layer. It uses an online-panel survey of 2,110 UK adults and self-reported exposure, confidence, regret, and known harms; it does not verify misinformation, clinically confirm outcomes, establish causality, estimate population prevalence beyond the sample design, or evaluate an intervention.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Full LSHTM report reviewed for survey design, confidence gradients, information sources, topic exposure, regret and known harm, checking behavior, policy priorities, and limitations.
